l: Wrath of the Lord, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: The Chorus calls for the Wrath of the Lord to come visibly for doom and deed. It asks that Pentheus be struck until his throat and heart bleed.

l: Loveliness, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: The Chorus asks whether Loveliness should not be loved forever. Loveliness is associated with divine grace, freedom from fear, and the beautiful life of the wild lands.

l: God's judgment, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: God's judgment is said to wait for those who worship the Ruthless Will and for proud dreams that make things greater without God. The Chorus presents it as slow but unfailing.

l: the Spirit of God, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, DIONYSUS
s: The Spirit of God is described as the enduring law that remains strong through the ages. The Chorus says that human plans and efforts are vain when they strive beyond its laws.

l: Hippolytus; The Bacchae, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: A Messenger reports that Pentheus was killed on Kithaeron by Agave, Ino, Autonoë, and the Maenads after Dionysus revealed him and commanded his punishment. Agave returns carrying Pentheus's head, believing it to be a lion's head, but Cadmus leads her to recognize the truth and shows her Pentheus's body. Dionysus then appears, declares that the suffering is punishment for rejecting his divinity, and announces the future exile and transformation of Cadmus and his family. Agave and Cadmus leave Thebes in grief, while the Chorus reflects that divine outcomes often differ from human expectation.

l: Messenger, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: The Messenger reports Pentheus's death on Kithaeron. He describes how Dionysus bent a pine tree for Pentheus to climb, revealed him to the Maenads, and how Agave and the others tore him apart.

l: Agave, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Agave returns from Kithaeron in a state of ecstatic madness, carrying Pentheus's head and believing she has hunted a lion. Cadmus brings her back to recognition, after which she understands that she and her sisters killed Pentheus and accepts that Dionysus has punished their house.

l: Cadmus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Cadmus searches for and recovers Pentheus's scattered body, then helps Agave recognize the head she carries. Dionysus condemns Cadmus and his family to suffering, and Cadmus is destined to become a serpent-like figure and lead a conquering horde before reaching the Islands of the Blest with Harmonia.

l: Pentheus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Pentheus climbs a pine tree to see the Maenads, but Dionysus exposes him to them as an enemy. Agave, Ino, Autonoë, and the other Maenads tear him apart after he begs his mother to recognize him.

l: Dionysus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Dionysus directs the Maenads against Pentheus and later appears to Cadmus and Agave. He declares that their suffering is the punishment for mocking and denying his divinity, and he announces the future fate of Cadmus and his family.

l: Maenads, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: The Maenads hold ecstatic rites on Kithaeron and attack Pentheus after Dionysus commands them to avenge his rejection. They pull down the pine tree, pursue Pentheus, and help tear him apart.

l: Cadmus' daughters, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Cadmus' daughters, including Agave, Ino, and Autonoë, are driven into a Dionysian frenzy on Kithaeron. They seize Pentheus and participate in his dismemberment, bringing ruin upon their family.

l: Thebes, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Thebes is portrayed as the home of the royal family that has rejected Dionysus. Its people witness the consequences of that rejection, while Agave and Cadmus depart and leave the house disgraced.

l: Kithaeron, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Kithaeron is the mountainous place where Pentheus goes to observe the Maenads and where Dionysus delivers him to their vengeance. His body is torn apart and scattered through its ravines and woodland.

l: Pentheus's head, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Pentheus's head is carried from Kithaeron by Agave, who mistakes it for the head of a lion and intends to display it on the palace. Cadmus makes her look at it until she recognizes it as the head of her son.

l: Pentheus's body, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Pentheus's body is found by Cadmus after a difficult search through Kithaeron. It has been torn limb from limb, and Cadmus carries its remains back to Thebes on a bier.

l: Bacchic frenzy, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Bacchic frenzy makes Agave, Ino, Autonoë, and the other women mistake Pentheus for a wild beast and attack him without recognizing him. Agave's frenzy later clears when Cadmus questions her and makes her see the head she carries.

l: Pentheus's death, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Pentheus's death occurs when the Maenads pull down the pine tree and tear him apart. The Messenger presents it as the result of Dionysus's command and Pentheus's opposition to the god.

l: the hunt on Kithaeron, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: The hunt on Kithaeron is presented by Agave as a triumphant capture of a lion, though the supposed prey is Pentheus. It is actually the divinely directed pursuit that leads to his death and dismemberment.

l: the tearing apart of Pentheus, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: The tearing apart of Pentheus is carried out by Agave, Ino, Autonoë, and the Maenads. His arms, legs, flesh, and other parts are scattered through the mountain woodland, while Agave carries away his head.

l: Dionysian worship, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Dionysian worship appears through the Maenads' dances, songs, ivy, thyrsi, and ecstatic rites on Kithaeron. The Chorus praises Dionysus, while Dionysus insists that Thebes must recognize his divine status.

l: Justice, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Divine justice is shown in Pentheus's punishment for scorning Dionysus and in the suffering imposed on Cadmus's family. Dionysus states that the punishment follows their denial and mockery of his godhead.

l: truth and recognition, Hippolytus; The Bacchae, [_Enter hastily a_ MESSENGER _from the Mountain, pale and distraught._]
s: Truth and recognition emerge when Cadmus leads Agave from her belief that she carries a lion's head to the knowledge that it is Pentheus's head. Her recovery of memory and understanding transforms her triumph into grief and reveals the reality of the slaughter.

l: Hecuba and other plays
s: The document is a sequence of tragic and satyric dramatic records centered on the aftermath and wider consequences of Troy’s fall, the sufferings of Trojan survivors, and the destructive force of divine will, war, vengeance, and unstable fortune. It begins with Hecuba: Polydore’s ghost exposes Polymestor’s murder for Priam’s gold, while the Greeks sacrifice Polyxena. Hecuba receives both children’s bodies, wins Agamemnon’s covert support, and uses Trojan women to kill Polymestor’s sons and blind him; Agamemnon judges him guilty. It then follows Hercules’ family under Lycus’s tyranny. Hercules returns from the Underworld, kills Lycus, but Iris and a Fiend, acting for Juno, drive him mad so that he kills Megara and his children. Theseus persuades the devastated Hercules to live and accept refuge in Athens. The children of Hercules subsequently seek sanctuary in Athens from Eurystheus. Macaria offers herself to save Athens and her brothers; the allies defeat Eurystheus, who is captured and executed at Alcmene’s command despite an oracle concerning his burial. At Troy, Rhesus arrives too late to aid Hector and is killed at night by Ulysses and Diomede; the Muse promises his restoration as a god. The Trojan-captive records depict Cassandra’s assignment to Agamemnon, Andromache’s loss of Astyanax, Hecuba’s enslavement to Ulysses, Polyxena’s death, Helen’s confrontation with Hecuba and Menelaus, Astyanax’s burial, and Troy’s burning. Ulysses’ encounter with Polypheme follows: he gives the Cyclops wine, blinds him after Polypheme devours Greeks, and escapes. A separate Helen narrative clears Helen of blame: a phantom went to Troy while the real Helen remained faithful in Egypt. Reunited with shipwrecked Menelaus, she deceives Theoclymenus with a false funeral, escapes by sea, and is vindicated by Castor and Pollux. The final records return to Andromache in captivity in Phthia. Menelaus and Hermione threaten her and her son Molossus, but Peleus saves them. Hermione flees with Orestes, who has arranged Neoptolemus’ death. After Neoptolemus is killed at Apollo’s temple, Thetis orders his burial, directs Andromache and Molossus to a future with Helenus, and promises Peleus immortality.

l: Polydore, Hecuba and other plays
s: Polydore is the youngest son of Priam and Hecuba. As a child and royal refugee, Priam secretly sends him to Polymestor in Thrace, entrusting him to the Thracian king’s protection and fostering and providing gold for his support. After Troy’s fall, Polymestor, Polydore’s supposed friend and host, murders him for the gold, also preventing him from restoring Troy. His body is cast into the sea and lies unburied on the Thracian shore, denied funeral rites. After death he appears as a ghost, seeking burial from Hecuba. A servant finds his corpse, Hecuba recognizes Polymestor’s crime, and Agamemnon permits Polydore’s remains to be buried with Polyxena.

l: Hecuba, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hecuba is a former queen of Troy, Ilion, and Phrygia; Priam’s former wife; Cisseus’s daughter; and mother of Hector, Paris, Cassandra, Polyxena, Polydore, Astyanax, and other Trojan royal children. After Troy’s destruction, Priam is slain, Hector dies in the war, and Hecuba becomes an aged, physically decrepit captive and slave without city or children. She is allotted to Ulysses, while Cassandra is assigned to Agamemnon and Andromache to Achilles’ son. Despite her loss and enslavement, she reflects on the constancy of virtue and moral character. Her suffering centers on the deaths and threatened deaths of her family. A foreboding dream concerns her children. She appeals to Ulysses to spare Polyxena, but Polyxena is sacrificed at Achilles’ tomb; Hecuba praises her courage and orders her body protected and washed. She mourns Priam, Hector, Polyxena, Polydore, Cassandra’s captivity, Astyanax, her city, and her lost royal status. She advises Andromache to submit to Neoptolemus and preserve Astyanax, then learns the Greeks have ordered the boy killed. After mourning his mutilated body, she adorns him with the poor gifts available and performs his funeral rites before being taken into slavery under Ulysses. Hecuba also confronts Helen, accusing her of willingly following Paris for beauty and Troy’s wealth, rejecting advice to flee, and remaining proud rather than remorseful; she urges Menelaus to kill her. When Polydore is found dead, Hecuba identifies him as her son and asks Agamemnon to punish Polymestor for murder and denying burial. She deceives Polymestor with a promise to reveal Priam’s buried treasure. Assisted by Trojan women, she kills Polymestor’s sons and blinds him, then defends the revenge before Agamemnon, who accepts that Polymestor deserves punishment. Finally, Bacchus’s prophecy destines her to become a dog, and her tomb is known by that transformed form.

l: Polyxena, Hecuba and other plays
s: Polyxena is Hecuba’s daughter, sister of Polydore and Hector, a royal-born princess of Troy, and an unmarried virgin. After Troy’s fall, the Greeks take her captive and vote to sacrifice her at Achilles’ tomb as a gift to the dead. Rather than face purchase into slavery or dishonor, she chooses death. Led away by Ulysses and dragged to the tomb, she refuses restraint, asks to die as one born free, and exposes her breast and neck for the fatal blow. After she is slain, Andromache shrouds and mourns her, the Greeks provide foliage, a pyre, and offerings, and her remains await washing and interment. Hecuba seeks to delay burial so Polyxena may share a fire and grave with her dead son.

l: Ulysses, Hecuba and other plays
s: Ulysses is a Greek warrior, chief, hero, and king of Ithaca, son of Laertes, whose fluent speech, courage, and strategic action shape both the Trojan War and his troubled departure from it. Supported by Minerva through many toils, he serves as a spy in Troy, allies with Diomede in a night raid, kills Rhesus, takes his chariot, horses, and Dolon’s weapons, and escapes the Trojan camp. He also steals Minerva’s image. After Troy’s fall, he obeys the Greek order to escort Polyxena to sacrifice and persuades the army that Achilles must be honored. He persuades the Greeks to condemn Astyanax, then receives Hecuba as a captive slave by lot. Cassandra foretells that he will remain away from home for ten more years and suffer dangers at sea, abroad, and at his house. Storms drive his ship from Troy to Sicily, where he seeks provisions for his faithful companions but is trapped by Polyphemus. After the Cyclops kills some of his men, Ulysses uses wine to intoxicate him, directs an escape plan, blinds him with a heated olive pole, reveals his name, and hastens back toward the shore.

l: Achilles, Hecuba and other plays
s: Achilles is Peleus’s famed son, a Greek chief and the greatest Greek warrior. Angry with the chiefs, he refuses to assist the Argive host. In the Trojan War he kills Hector and drags Hector’s body around Troy’s walls. He is father of Neoptolemus and is also invoked as father of Molossus by family lineage. He dies for Greece at Troy, killed by Paris’s shaft, though others blame the Phrygians, Helen, or Menelaus. After death, his ghost appears at his tomb demanding Polyxena’s sacrifice; later he dwells on an Euxine-washed island.

l: Polymestor, Hecuba and other plays
s: Polymestor is a Thracian king, Priam’s friend, Hecuba’s guest-friend, and fosterer of Polydore after Priam sends the boy from Troy with gold. Once Troy falls, he murders Polydore with a sword to keep the entrusted gold, casts the body into the sea without a tomb, and violates hospitality. He later admits the killing to Hecuba. In revenge, Hecuba and Trojan women kill his sons and blind him. He appeals to Thracians and Grecian troops, but Agamemnon rejects his justification and orders him cast onto a deserted island. His friendship with Hecuba becomes enmity through his betrayal, murder, and punishment.

l: Priam, Hecuba and other plays
s: Priam, a Trojan king and father of an illustrious race, is husband of Hecuba and father of Polydore. Once the happy king of Phrygia, he secretly entrusted Polydore to the Thracian king. The Greeks conquered his city, destroyed his household, killed him, and left him uninterred.

l: Hector, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hector is a Trojan warrior, commander, lord, and defender of Troy during its ten-year siege. A leading war figure and ally of Troy, he commands its army and walls, seeks intelligence on the Greek fleet by sending Dolon with the promise of Achilles’ steeds, and directs the night watch. When reports come from the Greek camp, he first thinks the Greeks are fleeing, then accepts Aeneas’s advice to send a spy. He welcomes Rhesus as an ally but reproaches his late arrival, acknowledging that Rhesus helped establish his throne; Hector assigns him a post, gives Apollo as watchword, and stations him outside the Phrygian lines until morning. After Rhesus is killed, Hector condemns the guards, cares for the wounded charioteer, and orders honorable burial. He is Paris’s brother, Andromache’s husband, and Astyanax’s father. Remembered as the bravest of the Phrygians and Troy’s pride, he is killed by Achilles; his body is dragged around the walls, and his death leaves Andromache captive and Astyanax condemned. His shield becomes Astyanax’s burial place.

l: Agamemnon, Hecuba and other plays
s: Agamemnon is a Greek monarch, commander, and leader of the Greek host. He commands the Greeks, sends Talthybius to Hecuba, and orders Polyxena’s sacrifice while allowing her to die freely. He has taken Cassandra as his prize, loves her despite her madness, and intends to make her his concubine; Cassandra foretells ruin for his house. When Hecuba reveals that Polymestor murdered Polydore, Agamemnon pities her and seeks revenge, but fears Greek blame because Polymestor is regarded as an ally. He secretly permits Hecuba’s plan, restrains possible Greek interference, and supports burial rites for Polydore, Polyxena, and Polymestor’s sons. After hearing both sides, he judges Polymestor guilty of murder for gold and exiles him to a deserted island.

l: Cassandra, Hecuba and other plays
s: Cassandra, Hecuba’s daughter, is Apollo’s inspired prophetess and priestess. She warns about Paris, foretells Troy’s fall and Ulysses’ perilous return, then becomes Agamemnon’s captive, concubine, and envisioned bride. Carrying a bridal torch, she predicts Agamemnon’s death, the fall of Atreus’ house, and her own death before leaving with Talthybius.

l: Helen, Hecuba and other plays
s: Helen is a Spartan and Greek royal woman, daughter of Leda and Tyndarus and also identified as daughter of Jove or Zeus, sister of Castor and Pollux, wife of Menelaus, and mother of Hermione. Renowned as the fairest bride, she is central to conflicting accounts of the Trojan disaster. In one account she is a captive among Trojan women after the Greeks' victory, hated and accused of adultery, abduction, and causing the deaths and destruction associated with Troy. Dragged from the tents, she defends herself before Hecuba and Menelaus: Venus, Paris, Priam, and divine compulsion caused her departure, and Deiphobus forced her into marriage after Paris died. Menelaus nevertheless orders her taken to Greece for execution. Another account makes her guiltless: Juno sent an image, Helen’s eidolon, to Troy, while Hermes took the true Helen to Egypt to preserve her chastity. She never visits Troy, yet her name is slandered throughout Greece. In Egypt she lives as a suppliant near Proteus’s tomb, protected by its refuge, faithful to Menelaus, and pursued by Theoclymenus, who seeks to marry her. Hearing that Menelaus may be dead, she mourns, fears for her reputation and family, and considers suicide. Menelaus arrives, learns of the phantom, and is reunited with her when it vanishes. Helen then faces danger from Theoclymenus and warns Menelaus that Theonoe’s brother may kill him. She appeals to Theonoe for secrecy, refuses to become the king’s bride, and devises their escape: she pretends Menelaus has died, performs mourning and funeral rites, and obtains a ship and sailors for a supposed funeral voyage. She and her living husband board the Sidonian ship and escape Egypt by sea. Castor and Pollux declare that she will later be honored as a goddess. Later descriptions again condemn her as having fled with Paris and caused the Greek expedition, while Menelaus maintains that the gods, not her consent, plunged her into suffering and that sparing her was wise.

l: Paris, Hecuba and other plays
s: Paris is a Phrygian prince, son of Priam and Hecuba and brother of Hector, portrayed as a royal swain and wanderer. At Ida he judges the contest among Juno, Minerva, and Venus, choosing Venus as most beautiful and receiving Helen as his reward. He sails to Sparta, where accounts say he takes Helen, or Helen’s phantom, to Troy; he is also described as her youthful paramour. This act causes the Trojan War and is repeatedly linked to Troy’s ruin, the sufferings of the Phrygian women, and calamities in Greece. In the conflict, Venus protects him, while Minerva, disguised as Venus, persuades him to return to his station after he seeks Hector. Paris also kills Achilles with a missile shaft. His story thus moves from the judgment and voyage for Helen to a war whose disasters are attributed to his choice and abduction.

l: Peleus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Peleus is an aged but capable king, descended from Aeacus, husband of Thetis, father of Achilles, and grandfather of Achilles’ son, Neoptolemus, as well as of Molossus through Achilles. A veteran ruler of Phthia who also rules Pharsalia, he bears a sceptre as authority. When Andromache and Molossus face death, he arrives, has their chains removed, condemns Menelaus, and shelters them; he had also protected them from Hermione’s attack. Though others question his age, he asserts that courage can surpass youth. Later he learns that Hermione has fled and that Achilles’ son was murdered at Delphi. Having already lost Achilles, he mourns his grandson and his childlessness. Thetis consoles him, directs burial of the body, and transforms him into an immortal, incorruptible being.

l: Theseus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Theseus is a king of Athens and kinsman and friend of Hercules, bound by gratitude after Hercules rescued him from the underworld. He commands Athenian youths and holds land throughout Athens’ realm. Expected as help in Hercules’ grief, he arrives after the slaughter, comforts him, rejects contagious pollution, offers refuge, wealth, purification, and honor in Athens, and leads him from Thebes.

l: Jove, Hecuba and other plays
s: Jove is a god and supreme ruler of Heaven, described as ruling inferior gods, authoring success and divine judgments, and punishing base deeds and pride. He is father of Hercules, Hebe, and Helen, grandfather of Hermione, and father of Hercules’ children through Hercules. His altar, erected by Hercules, protects Hercules’ family, and he is invoked for their defense. He aids Athens against Argos and overthrows Troy. Yet Amphitryon and the Chorus question his justice and hatred when he does not save Hercules or his children. By the end, he is invoked as Zeus for victory and renewed strength.

l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Chorus is a group whose membership and role shift across the records, but whose central work is collective witnessing, lament, counsel, praise, and moral response. It includes captive Trojan women serving the Greek army and attending Hecuba; aged men who stand with Amphitryon; Trojan guards on a night watch; Phrygian women mourning Troy; the sons of Bacchus enslaved by Polyphemus; and observers of the dispute involving Andromache and Molossus. It repeatedly gives voice to people endangered, defeated, enslaved, or grieving. It begins with the captive women of Troy: they bring Hecuba news that Polyxena will be sacrificed, share her grief, lament Troy’s destruction, support her against Helen, and recount the wooden horse, slaughter, burning, enslavement, lost homes, husbands, children, shrines, and sacrifices. They also help prepare Astyanax’s funeral ornaments and fear assignment to Greek masters. Elsewhere, aged men praise Hercules, oppose Lycus, celebrate restored hope, and then fear fresh evil; they also hope Athens will protect strangers against Argos and praise Macaria’s willingness to die. During the night watch, the Trojan guards praise Rhesus, pray for Greek defeat, track the guards, fear for Dolon, pursue the night raiders, hear the charioteer, witness the dispute with Hector, respond to the Muse’s lament, and prepare to obey Hector. The sons of Bacchus, deprived of wine and enslaved by Polyphemus, welcome Ulysses’ plan to blind him but evade direct help by feigning injuries. Toward the end, Chorus acts most plainly as a moral commentator: it pities Andromache and Molossus, opposes their execution as unjust, urges reconciliation, announces Peleus, and calls for an end to quarrelling. Its songs condemn divided households and rival wives, while praising inherited nobility, lawful victory, virtue, and power without crime. Across all these appearances, it supports justice, retribution, compassion, and endurance amid changing fortune.

l: the Greeks, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Greeks are the Greek or Argive army and host assembled at Troy under leaders including Menelaus, Agamemnon, Achilles, Ajax, Tydeus’ son, Ulysses, and Diomede. They wage the Trojan War against Troy over Helen, endure many deaths before its walls, and are said by Menelaus to become valiant through the war. During the conflict they occupy a camp and fleet near Troy, kindle fires that alarm Trojan guards, and send Ulysses and Diomede into the Trojan camp, where they kill Rhesus. They ultimately deceive Troy with the wooden horse, storm and sack it with spear and fire, kill its defenders, take spoils, and become victorious. They capture, divide by lot, and enslave Trojan women, including Hecuba; kill Astyanax because they fear he may rebuild Ilion; and prepare to burn the city. After the fall, the army remains encamped in the Thracian Chersonesus while unfavorable conditions delay its return to Greece. By general consent it resolves to sacrifice Polyxena at Achilles’ tomb, carries out the killing, and then honors her corpse with foliage, a pyre, and ornaments. It treats Polymestor as an ally despite Hecuba’s dead son being regarded as an enemy, and Agamemnon declines to aid Polymestor after his blinding. The host assigns captives and prepares its homeward voyage, but Minerva and Neptune plan storms and destruction at sea; later, the returning fleet is wrecked by Nauplius’s deceptive beacon at Caphareus. Greeks accompanying Menelaus also fight Egyptians aboard a ship and prevail.

l: gods, Hecuba and other plays
s: The gods are a group of divine powers invoked to hear holy prayers, recognize broken trust, protect communities, grant victory and guidance, determine fate, and control unstable human fortune. At the outset they are associated with restored ancient honours, peace, order, and the punishment of neglected laws; Hercules is said to have restored their honours. Their authority is also presented as requiring punishment of Hercules, since Iris and the Fiend claim they would lose power if he escaped. As suffering intensifies, they become contested: Hercules questions whether true gods need support or commit the crimes attributed to them, while Theseus urges reverence. They demand a noble maiden’s sacrifice, punish violated temples through Minerva and Neptune, and inspire Cassandra through Apollo. Hecuba and the Chorus portray them as bringing Troy overwhelming suffering and as unreliable or false. Finally, they are blamed for Helen’s deception, Menelaus’s hardships, and sudden reversals of fortune.

l: Thracian Chersonesus, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_a land [fruitful Thracian territory] The Thracian Chersonesus is the coast where the Greek army is stationed after leaving Troy. It is also where Polymestor rules and where Polydore’s unburied corpse lies on the shore.

l: Thrace, Hecuba and other plays
s: Thrace is the realm ruled by the Thracian king, including Thracian Chersonesus. Priam sends Polydore there from Troy to be raised, but the king’s household becomes the setting of his murder, prompting Hecuba’s fear.

l: Troy, Hecuba and other plays
s: Troy is a wealthy, formerly prosperous Phrygian city, Priam’s city, situated on Scamander and once fortified by walls, towers, palaces, temples, shrines, sacrifices, and a citadel sacred to Neptune. What matters most is its transformation from a royal, protected, hospitable city into a ruined and nearly nameless site through the Greeks’ ten-year siege and war. Under Greek attack, Troy receives Rhesus and the Thracians as allies; Hector and the Chorus hope their aid will preserve the city, defeat the besiegers, and restore its celebrations. Rhesus’s loss reverses this hope, although Hector still imagines freeing Troy by attacking the Greek ramparts and fleet. The city ultimately falls to Menelaus and the Greek chiefs. Greek spear, war, and fire tear down its defenses, walls, palaces, streets, towers, and sanctuaries; its bulwarks smoke, its roofs and citadel burn, and no trace of its walls remains. Its rulers die or are reduced to captivity, its women enter servitude, and its dead, including Astyanax, are mourned. Hecuba foresees the disappearance of Troy’s illustrious name, while the Chorus says that even its memorials are lost. Its destruction is repeatedly linked to Helen, Paris’s taking of Helen, or a phantom resembling Helen; Menelaus and a messenger say the Greeks’ labors may therefore have been in vain. Yet the records consistently present Troy’s fall as a disaster whose suffering reaches both Phrygia and Greece.

l: Phrygia, Hecuba and other plays
s: Phrygia is a vanquished Asian city associated with Troy and Andromache’s homeland, containing Minerva’s temple. In the Trojan War’s fall of Troy, it is destroyed; Troy is conquered, burned, devastated, and its people and structures lost.

l: Athens, Hecuba and other plays
s: Athens is an independent, free city defined by its refusal to yield to Argive domination and its protection of foreign suppliants. It first offers Hercules refuge after his exile from Thebes, promising cleansing, a palace, wealth, and honors after his death. Later it protects his sons despite the threat of Eurystheus’ Argive army. Though its people disagree, it arms, performs sacrifices and lustrations, and chooses not to betray its guests. Athens defeats Eurystheus’ forces, spares him out of reverence for the gods, and receives the promise that his buried corpse will guard the city.

l: Sparta, Hecuba and other plays
s: Sparta is a realm and homeland associated chiefly with Menelaus, Helen, and Hermione. Menelaus repeatedly seeks or begins a return there, while Helen, calling it her native realm and former home, hopes return with him will restore her standing among the Greeks and recover her former life after a false reputation of guilt. It is also the place from which Menelaus comes to aid Hermione and from which he plans to lead forces against a neighboring enemy. Its stature is invoked by Hermione, but Andromache denounces its inhabitants as treacherous, and Peleus criticizes the customs of Spartan women.

l: the Underworld, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Underworld is Pluto’s realm beneath the earth, a house of tears containing spirits and Cerberus. It is Pluto’s gloomy mansion of shades, ruled by stern law, where Charon’s boat carries the dead to an eternal home from which they do not normally return. Hercules enters through Taenarus, brings Cerberus into the light, rescues Theseus, and returns after a prolonged stay.

l: Achilles’ tomb, Hecuba and other plays
s: Achilles’ tomb is a sepulchre and the site claimed for Polyxena’s sacrifice. Achilles’ ghost appears there, demanding a Trojan captive. Polyxena is assigned there, first thought to be sepulchral service, then taken and killed as a gift to Achilles.

l: Agamemnon’s tent, Hecuba and other plays
s: Agamemnon’s tent stands in the Greek camp near Troy and serves as the place where Hecuba and the captive women are held. Talthybius comes from it to announce the captives’ assignments.

l: Polydore’s corpse, Hecuba and other plays
s: Polydore’s corpse has been cast into the sea and left unwept and unburied on the rocky shore. Polydore’s ghost seeks honorable burial and intends that Hecuba’s servant perform the rites.

l: Priam’s treasure, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_kept_by Polymestor [in Polymestor’s palace] Polydore’s gold was brought from Troy and kept by Polymestor in his palace. Hecuba uses the promise of additional Priamite treasure to draw Polymestor into the tent, while Agamemnon concludes that greed for the gold motivated Polydore’s murder.

l: the Greek fleet, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Greek fleet lies near the hostile shore, marked by torches and fires and protected by Achilles against Trojan attack. Dolon is sent to reconnoitre its trenches and ramparts, while Rhesus and Hector threaten to burn it. It later waits near Troy to carry away the victorious host and captive women as Minerva and Neptune prepare storms to destroy or scatter it.

l: Polyxena’s sacrifice, Hecuba and other plays
s: Polyxena’s sacrifice is a rite at Achilles’ tomb, demanded by his appearing ghost and approved by the Greek army to propitiate him and allow the Greeks to depart Troy safely. Though Hecuba tries to replace or save her, Polyxena freely accepts her assigned death. Achilles’ son performs the sacrifice; Polyxena bleeds and dies, then the Greeks honor her while Andromache shrouds her.

l: the fall and destruction of Troy, Hecuba and other plays
s: The fall and destruction of Troy is the Greek victory over the city, caused by the wooden-horse deception and followed by the destruction of its walls, slaughter, fire, and captivity. It reduces Troy to smoke, flame, nameless ruins: its royal house is destroyed, its memorials and even its name disappear, and no trace of its once-proud walls remains. Hector and Priam die; Hecuba loses her husband, children, city, and freedom; and the Trojan women are enslaved and dragged from their homeland. With Troy’s protection gone, Polymestor murders Polydore. The Grecian forces then depart on their return voyage to Greece. The destruction occurred nearly seven years before the present.

l: Trojan War, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Trojan War is a ten-year Greek siege and assault at Troy, fought to recover Helen, though some accounts say Juno replaced her with a phantom and that Greeks and Trojans suffered for an image. Paris’s taking of Helen is also given as its cause. The conflict brings Greek warriors to Troy and continues ineffectually for ten years; Rhesus claims his arrival will end it, while Hector urges attention to Troy’s immediate danger. It kills many Greeks and Trojans, leaves widows, fathers, wives, husbands, and households grieving, and gives generals and rulers glory and reputation while soldiers bear the labor and suffering. Ulysses recalls the dangers endured, and Polypheme and the Chorus condemn the war’s dishonor and the doubtful value of fame and victory gained through slaughter. It ends when the Greeks overthrow Troy’s towers, destroy the city, capture the land, and prepare to return home.

l: Polydore’s murder, Hecuba and other plays
s: Polydore’s murder is Polymestor’s killing of the boy Priam entrusted to him, motivated by Priam’s gold and violating hospitality. Polymestor throws the body into the sea; it reaches shore and is brought to Hecuba. Polymestor later confesses, Hecuba’s account convinces Agamemnon, and the murder prompts justice and revenge.

l: Hecuba’s dream, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hecuba dreams of a wolf tearing a dappled hind from her arms, and she understands the vision as a warning concerning Polydore and Polyxena. She also sees Achilles’ ghost demanding a Trojan captive.

l: the enslavement of Hecuba and the Trojan women, Hecuba and other plays
s: The enslavement of Hecuba and the Trojan women is a captivity following Troy’s destruction. Torn from the royal household, Hecuba remains enslaved and is assigned to Ulysses as Polyxena is taken to die. Hecuba, Andromache, and other women are carried from their land to Greece for forced, degrading service.

l: slavery, Hecuba and other plays
s: Slavery is the condition imposed on conquered Trojan women after Troy’s destruction. Polyxena rejects survival under it, choosing death to preserve freedom from dishonor. Hecuba, Andromache, and others face degrading service or forced relationships despite noble birth; Andromache’s enslavement to Neoptolemus silences her and makes resistance dangerous.

l: death, Hecuba and other plays
s: Death is preferred by Polyxena to ignoble slavery, takes Priam, Hector, and Trojan defenders, and leaves Hecuba grieving captivity. It then unites Megara, her children, and Amphitryon in descent to Pluto’s realm, as Amphitryon accepts their fate.

l: Talthybius, Hecuba and other plays
s: Talthybius is a herald, messenger, and Greek troop leader serving the Greeks. He carries Agamemnon’s orders and announces the captives’ assignments, Cassandra’s delivery to Agamemnon, Polyxena’s sacrifice, and Astyanax’s execution. Though reluctant when telling Andromache of the decree against her son, he urges compliance so Astyanax may receive funeral honors. After Neoptolemus leaves Astyanax’s body with Hecuba, Talthybius washes it, prepares and helps dig the grave, and directs the Greeks’ work on the tomb. At the end he orders Greek troops to burn Troy and commands Hecuba to follow Ulysses.

l: Neoptolemus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Neoptolemus is Achilles’ son and Peleus’ grandson, associated with Phthia and the spoils of Troy. After Troy’s fall, he takes the captive Andromache as his wife and travels with her to Phthia; he also permits Astyanax’s body to be given to Hecuba for burial. He later marries Hermione, yet is said to love Andromache. While he is away at Delphi seeking expiation from Apollo and reparation for Achilles’ death, Andromache and Molossus are threatened. He scorns Orestes, refusing Orestes’ request to release Hermione and reproaching him for killing his mother. Orestes prepares his death: Neoptolemus is lured to Apollo’s temple at Delphi, attacked by Delphi’s citizens with Orestes’ involvement, and fights in Achilles’ armor before being overwhelmed, killed, and mutilated. He is carried to Peleus, and Thetis commands his burial at Apollo’s temple at Delphi.

l: Venus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Venus, also called Aphrodite, is a goddess of love and beauty whose judgment by Paris drives the story. She promises him Helen as the prize for naming her fairest, wins the contest, and her promise brings Paris to Sparta, war, and suffering linked to Helen. Helen blames Venus for leaving Sparta, though Hecuba calls Venus a name for desire. Venus creates Helen’s eidolon and opposes Menelaus’s return, while Helen begs her to stop harming her house.

l: Minerva, Hecuba and other plays
s: Minerva is an invincible goddess, guardian and queen of Athens, who protects Ulysses and aids Greek aims against Troy. She directs Ulysses and Diomede against Rhesus, delays Paris in Venus’ form, and inspires Epeus to build the Trojan Horse. After Ajax violates her temple by seizing Cassandra, she seeks Neptune and Zeus’s force to ruin the Greeks’ return voyage.

l: the Trojans, Hecuba and other plays
s: inhabits Troy [the city is their homeland] The Trojans are represented through the destruction of their city and the loss of their royal household. Their homeland is conquered, their mansions are leveled, and the survivors are reduced to captivity and grief.

l: the Phrygian matrons, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Phrygian matrons are captive Trojan women and Hecuba’s attendants who form a chorus. They lament Troy’s destruction, their dead sons, husbands, and children, and recall Paris’s voyage and choice of Venus; by the end, they are taken to Greece for servitude and separation.

l: Phthia, Hecuba and other plays
s: Phthia is Peleus’s Thessalian realm and city, ruled by him with cavalry and infantry, though Neoptolemus is associated with its rule. Andromache arrives at its coast and lives there captive among Hector’s killers. Peleus vows to protect her and educate Molossus, defending the realm’s succession against Menelaus’s challenge. Hermione, living in Achilles’ son’s household, fears Phthia hates and will expel her after her attempted violence against Andromache. It ends with Peleus mourning its empty mansions and lost descendants.

l: Ida, Hecuba and other plays
s: Ida is the place where Hera, Aphrodite, and Pallas competed for the prize of beauty and asked Paris to judge them. Helen says that Paris later came from Ida to Sparta.

l: the Trojan War, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Trojan War is a ten-year conflict between Greeks and Trojans that ends in the Greek victory, the fall and sack of Troy, and the destruction of its walls. It is presented as arising from Helen and from Paris’s voyage from Sparta, his connection with Helen, his violation of hospitality, and his choice of Venus. During the war, Greeks besiege Troy while Troy seeks allied Thracian aid. In one phase, Hector believes Trojan success offers a chance to destroy the Greek ships, though Aeneas warns against a night engagement; Rhesus joins the Trojan formation and seeks to fight the Greeks, especially Ulysses. Greeks Ulysses and Diomede make a night attack on Rhesus as Hector prepares an assault on the Greek camp. The conflict culminates in the wooden-horse deception and Troy’s capture. Its consequences include deaths among Greeks and Trojans, including Trojan youths, the losses of Achilles and Ajax, the killing of Astyanax, burial of the dead, and the enslavement of Hecuba, Trojan women, and other survivors. Greek victors, including Menelaus’s companions, claim renown from Troy’s conquest.

l: the sack of Troy, Hecuba and other plays
s: The sack of Troy is a Greek victory achieved by Menelaus and the Greek chiefs after the Greeks, led by Menelaus, defeated and entered the city from a wooden horse. Its central consequence is Troy’s utter ruin: its men and royal family are killed, its palaces, temples, altars, sacred places, rites, and towers are destroyed or profaned, and its women become captives and slaves. Astyanax is thrown from the towers, and Andromache is taken from her home. Hecuba is reduced from queen to aged, childless slave, while the Trojan women mourn and are carried away. Menelaus claims the conquest from Priam, yet his sparing of Helen prompts criticism that the conflict caused needless deaths; Minerva and Neptune connect the Greeks’ treatment of Troy to their future punishment.

l: the judgment of Paris, Hecuba and other plays
s: The judgment of Paris is a contest over beauty among Hera, Aphrodite, and Athena, also called Juno, Venus, and Minerva. Paris judges the rivals and awards victory to Venus, who promises him Helen as his reward. The choice is presented as bringing vengeance from a foreign state and causing the Trojan War, though Hecuba rejects it as an excuse for Helen’s conduct.

l: Fortune, Hecuba and other plays
s: Fortune is a changeful, unstable power that governs human affairs and life through judgments linked to Fate, the gods, and Zeus’s ordination. It reverses prosperity and suffering: no one remains permanently blessed or afflicted, and it can take away all former glory in a day. Its force makes human plans and boasts vain, assigns harsh destinies in place of hoped-for marriages, and shapes Menelaus’s fortunes and delayed return. Yet its changes also leave room for hope that suffering may alter, though fate and necessity cannot be prevented. From Troy’s ruin and disputed divine causes to Peleus’s imposed suffering and humanity’s debt of death, Fortune unfolds as the source of unexpected reversals under divine guidance.

l: hospitality, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hospitality is a law recognized by mankind and associated with the gods. Offered to Rhesus by Troy, it is invoked by Ulysses to demand shelter and aid from Polypheme, who rejects it by eating guests; Ulysses warns that such defiance brings ruin.

l: Neptune, Hecuba and other plays
s: Neptune, a god, helps Apollo build Troy, loves it, then leaves its ruined, deserted temples and joins Minerva to punish the returning Greeks with storms, waves, and whirlpools.

l: Trojan women, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Trojan women are captives of Grecian troops after Troy’s fall. Concealed in tents, they join Hecuba’s punishment of Polymestor, killing his sons and blinding him, then leave for their lords’ tents to endure hardship.

l: Trojans, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Trojans inhabit Troy and suffer warfare, slaughter, and the loss of Rhesus and his troops. Hector orders mourning, burial, arming, and preparation for assault. After Greek attack destroys their city and kills many, they bring a wooden horse into Troy as a pledge of peace; Greeks concealed within emerge and begin Troy’s destruction.

l: fate and the Destinies, Hecuba and other plays
s: Fate and the Destinies are an uncontrollable divine force governing human fortunes, events, prophecy, and outcomes beyond human power. They turn intended marriages into deathly unions: for Megara, they are brides given to Hercules’ sons, bringing tears rather than happiness. They prevent Ulysses and Diomede from killing Hector or Paris, ordain the deaths of Rhesus and his allies, and reserve Achilles for an inevitable shaft. They can overturn noble birth into slavery, as in the sufferings of Hecuba and Andromache. Through divine councils, including Jove’s, they determine events such as Helen’s departure and ensure that the gods produce unexpected, perplexing results.

l: Ilion, Hecuba and other plays
s: Ilion is a formerly prosperous city, also called Troy and Pergamus, whose defeat and destruction by the Greeks define its record. After the Greek assault, it is captured, burned, leveled, and overthrown; smoke rises as its towers, temples, royal houses, streets, altars, and customs are ruined. Priam, his sons, and Polyxena are among the dead, while Hecuba, other women, and children lose their city and are enslaved, carried into captivity, or killed. Ulysses links its wasting to vengeance.

l: revenge and retaliation, Hecuba and other plays
s: Revenge and retaliation is a principle used to justify punishment and sought by Hecuba against Polymestor for murdering her son and violating guest obligations. It unfolds through Hecuba’s secretly supported plan for Trojan women to act, while Menelaus calls retaliation just and Andromache condemns punishment of the uninvolved.

l: Justice, Hecuba and other plays
s: Justice is a divine and universal law requiring punishment for transgression and restoration for violated obligations. It unfolds through Hecuba’s and Agamemnon’s demand that Polymestor be punished for murdering Polydore, then through the Chorus’s portrayal of Lycus’s death as repayment for violence, blasphemy, and unjust rule. Finally, it guides Theonoe to protect Menelaus and Helen, uphold her father’s honor, and respect plighted trust despite her brother’s demand.

l: funeral rites, Hecuba and other plays
s: are_performed_for Polyxena [before the burial of Hecuba’s dead son] Agamemnon says that the appropriate rites for Polyxena have been performed and agrees to delay her burial. He permits Polyxena and Hecuba’s dead son to be consumed in one fire and buried together.

l: Cassandra’s relationship with Agamemnon, Hecuba and other plays
s: Cassandra’s enslavement to Agamemnon is announced as her assignment as his concubine rather than as an ordinary slave. She responds by performing a mock bridal celebration and prophesying that the union will bring disaster to Agamemnon and his house.

l: Hecuba’s suffering, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_extreme the greatest among mortals [as Hecuba presents it] Hecuba presents her suffering as unparalleled: she has lost her sons, her city, her royal status, and her freedom. She is now old, enslaved, and deprived of her children, with Polyxena newly dead and her remaining hope focused on vengeance.

l: women’s schemes, Hecuba and other plays
s: are_used_against Polymestor [by Hecuba and the Trojan women] Hecuba claims that women’s wiles are difficult to resist and that their numbers can terrify an enemy. She intends to use these means, together with the Trojan women concealed in the tents, against Polymestor.

l: Greek homeward voyage, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Greek homeward voyage is prepared after captives are assigned and the fleet receives plunder. It is to carry Helen from Troy to Greece for death, but Minerva and Neptune plan thunder, winds, waves, and shipwreck, while the Chorus prays lightning destroys the ship.

l: sons of Polymestor, Hecuba and other plays
s: Polymestor’s sons are present when Hecuba reveals the supposed location of Priam’s treasure. The Trojan women separate them from their father and kill them with concealed swords.

l: the Thracians, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Thracians are Rhesus's immense army and Trojan allies in the Trojan War. After campaigning against the Scythians, they march by night around Ida to aid Troy, bringing horses, shield-bearers, archers, and infantry. Hector assigns Apollo as their emergency watchword. That night, Rhesus and much of the force are destroyed; his wounded charioteer reports it.

l: Greece, Hecuba and other plays
s: Greece is a place central to the aftermath and memory of the war against Troy. It sent warriors and ships, endured ten years of conflict, and suffered the deaths of many leaders and other losses associated with Helen’s phantom and reputation. It is the homeland and intended return destination of Helen, Menelaus, and the returning Greek warriors, while captive Trojan women, including Hecuba and Andromache, are taken there; Andromache is assigned to Neoptolemus’ household. Menelaus plans to bring Helen to Greece and clear her name’s infamy. Greece is also invoked as a possible future invader of Thrace, though Hecuba rejects that claim as a pretext.

l: Argos, Hecuba and other plays
s: Argos is a city hostile to Athens, ruled by Eurystheus. It expels or pursues the children of Hercules, demanding their surrender and threatening invasion. Under Eurystheus it approaches Athens with numerous squadrons, then supplies the army fighting Athens and the children’s supporters, while its people are urged to defend their native land.

l: Greek encampment, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Greek encampment, on the shore beside the Greek fleet, holds Trojan women captive in tents. Hecuba lures Polymestor into a tent by claiming to reveal treasure. At night, many fires and tumultuous troops moving toward Agamemnon’s tent create uncertainty about Greek intentions.

l: Polymestor’s sons’ corpses, Hecuba and other plays
s: The corpses of Polymestor’s sons are left exposed after the Trojan women kill them. Agamemnon orders that both corpses be deposited in a grave.

l: murder of Polymestor’s sons, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hecuba arranges the murder of Polymestor’s sons as revenge for Polydore’s murder. The Trojan women hold Polymestor and stab his sons with swords concealed beneath their garments.

l: blinding of Polymestor, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hecuba and the Trojan women blind Polymestor after killing his sons. He emerges from the tent unable to see, searches for his attackers, and appeals unsuccessfully to the Thracians and Grecian troops.

l: the voyage to Greece, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_guided_by the Dioscuri [they guide Helen and Menelaus over the waves] The voyage to Greece begins after the Greeks raise the mast and receive favorable winds. Castor and Pollux promise to guide Helen and Menelaus over the waves, while Menelaus is destined eventually to dwell among the happy islands.

l: Bacchus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Bacchus is a god of wine, pleasure, and revelry, associated with purple grapes and able to dwell as divine power wherever wine is lodged, even in a vessel. His wine gives pleasure and intoxication and is prized, traded, and used by Ulysses to persuade Polyphemus. Seized by Etrurian pirates, he is sought by Silenus and the Satyrs, honored in Bacchic ritual, invoked by Ulysses, and followed by the Chorus.

l: Amphitryon, Hecuba and other plays
s: Amphitryon is an aged, physically weakened man from Argos, descended from Alcaeus through Perseus’ son, and the father of Hercules and Megara. Once a doer of glorious deeds, he is reduced in one day from former glory to a refugee with Megara and Hercules’ children at Jupiter’s altar, threatened with death by Lycus. He defends Hercules’ courage, recounts his lineage and labours, appeals unsuccessfully to Zeus for rescue, and bitterly reproaches Jove for failing Hercules’ family. When Hercules returns, Amphitryon explains the danger and urges him to hide, expecting Lycus’ punishment. After Hercules, driven by madness, kills Megara and the children, Amphitryon grieves, fears for his own life, and carefully tells Hercules what happened. He urges Hercules to restrain himself, undertakes the children’s burial because Hercules may not perform it, and receives Hercules’ promise to bury him afterward.

l: Megara, Hecuba and other plays
s: Megara is the daughter of Creon, the deceased king of Thebes, and the wife and consort of Hercules, with whom she has children. She is a refugee at Jupiter’s altar with Amphitryon and her children when Lycus threatens them with execution. Grieving for the absent Hercules and seeing little hope of escape or persuasion, she asks that her sons be dressed in funeral robes and leads them with Amphitryon toward death. She recalls Hercules’ plans for their inheritances and marriages, appeals to him for protection, and condemns their attackers as cowards. When Hercules returns, she tells him of Lycus’s killings and threats, then enters the palace with him and the children after his promise of safety. During a purification ceremony, Hercules kills Megara and a child in madness. He later mourns her as faithful to his bed and watchful over his house.

l: Hercules, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hercules is a hero of extraordinary strength, a benefactor of Greece, and a figure defined by arduous service, family catastrophe, endurance, and eventual dwelling among the gods. He is identified as the son of Jove and also of Amphitryon, through Alcmena; he is Megara’s husband and the father of their children, with Macaria also counted among his children. He has a house in Thebes and is honored there by an altar of Jupiter for victory over the Minyans. For Eurystheus, Hercules performs labours intended to rid the world of pests. His deeds include slaying the Nemean lion and wearing its hide, subduing the Lernaean Hydra, killing Geryon, Cycnus, and the dragon of the Hesperian gardens, capturing the Ceryneian hind, mastering Diomedes’ man-eating horses and bringing them to Eurystheus, battling the Amazons while seeking Hippolita’s belt, relieving Atlas by carrying the heavens’ load, and wounding Centaurs. His final labour takes him into the Underworld, where he defeats and brings back Cerberus and rescues Theseus. While he is absent, Megara, Amphitryon, and his children are threatened by Lycus. Hercules returns, learns of the danger, and kills Lycus. Soon afterward, however, divine hostility sends him into madness. Mistaking his own family for Eurystheus’ children, he kills his children and Megara with his weapons. Athena stops the frenzy, and, when he wakes, he is bound, polluted by the murders, overwhelmed by grief and shame, and considers suicide. He cannot bury those he killed and must leave Thebes under its laws of pollution. Theseus persuades him to endure rather than die. Hercules agrees to live, keep his weapons, and depart after Amphitryon performs the burial. Later records remember him as dead but dwelling in heaven, restored among the gods and married to Hebe. His children continue to suffer exile and persecution because of their connection to him, while his courage, labours, rescue of Theseus, and service to Greece remain central to his memory.

l: Lycus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Lycus is a tyrant who becomes ruler of Thebes by invading amid civil tumult, murdering Creon, and seizing the throne. He seeks to prevent vengeance by ordering the execution of Megara, Amphitryon, and the children of Hercules, disparaging Hercules and planning to burn the family. Though he allows Megara to prepare the children, he enters the palace to bring them out and is killed there by Hercules in an ambush of swords.

l: Iris, Hecuba and other plays
s: Iris, the gods’ ambassadress, joins Juno against Hercules, orders a Fiend to drive him mad to kill his children, then departs for Olympus.

l: Juno, Hecuba and other plays
s: Juno, also called Hera, is Jove’s wife and a divine power of hostility, vengeance, and deception. Her inveterate rage against Hercules arises because Jove loved Alcmena; she sends the Fiend with Iris to drive him mad, causing him to kill his family and ruin his household. After losing the judgment of beauty, she opposes Paris by creating Helen’s likeness, sending the real Helen to Egypt, and making Greeks and Trojans fight over the phantom. Though formerly hostile to Menelaus, she later favors him, Helen, and their safe return to Sparta.

l: Creon, Hecuba and other plays
s: Creon, Menoeceus’ son, is Thebes’ former king and Megara’s father; Lycus kills him, seizes Thebes, and fears Hercules’ children will avenge him.

l: Eurystheus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Eurystheus is a king and tyrant of Argos and Mycenae, a foe of Alcmene, Hercules, and Hercules’ sons. He commands Hercules to bring captive horses, then, after Hercules’ death, pursues the children from city to city, sends Copreus to seize them, and seeks their murder because they may avenge their father. Waiting near Alcathous’ realm, he threatens Athens and leads an Argive army against it. He refuses Hyllus’s challenge, is defeated, captured, chained, and brought before Alcmene. As a suppliant, he accepts Athens’ protection and gives Phoebus’s oracle that his buried corpse will guard Athens against Hercules’ descendants, becoming its guardian after death.

l: Chorus of Theban old men, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Chorus is composed of aged Theban men, belonging to Thebes. Though too weak to fight, it loyally supports Amphitryon, Megara, and the children, opposes and condemns Lycus, and defends Hercules’ honor. It later laments Hercules’ frenzy and the deaths of Megara and the children, helps guard him, and condemns Jove and the gods.

l: children of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays
s: The children of Hercules are a group descended from Hercules and Megara, grandchildren of Amphitryon through Hercules. Their story begins under Lycus’s threat: sheltering with Megara and Amphitryon as suppliants at Jupiter’s altar, they await Hercules, while Lycus orders their execution out of fear that they will avenge Creon. Dressed in funeral garments, they are prepared as victims and imagined as bound for Charon’s boat and Pluto’s abode. Hercules returns, embraces them, and takes them into the palace to protect them. During a purification, however, he turns violent; the terrified children flee and hide, but he kills all three in the belief that they are Eurystheus’ children. Hercules mourns them, while Amphitryon must bury them and their tomb is to be visited and lamented. The records also present Hercules’ children as an exiled family pursued by Eurystheus from Argos and other Greek cities. Protected by Athens at Marathon, they seek safety at Jupiter’s altar under Iolaus. Demophoon refuses to surrender them, Macaria offers herself for their welfare, and their eventual victory frees them from Eurystheus’s rule, allowing them to return to their father’s city and inherit its fields. Their lost prospects include rule in Thebes and Oecalia and inheritance in Argos.

l: Thebes, Hecuba and other plays
s: Thebes is Cadmus’ city, founded by Cadmus, whose people descend from the dragon’s sown race; it contains Hercules’ house and Jupiter’s altar. Lycus invades after a revolt, kills Creon, seizes the throne, and rules amid violence, disorder, and condemnation. The city later rejoices at restoration of its rightful king. After killings, its laws exclude Hercules; citizens are asked to mourn as Theseus leads him away toward Athens.

l: altar of Jupiter, Hecuba and other plays
s: The altar of Jupiter is a protective sanctuary erected by Hercules to memorialize victory over the Minyans. It provides asylum to Hercules’ children and other threatened suppliants, including Amphitryon and Megara, despite their deprivation. At Marathon, Copreus tries to remove them, but the Chorus and Demophoon defend its inviolability.

l: Hercules’ house, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_in Thebes [at the entrance to the house] Hercules’ house in Thebes is closed against Megara, Amphitryon, and the children while Lycus threatens them. Lycus orders its gates opened so Megara can take the children inside and dress them in funeral robes before their execution.

l: the Labours of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Labours of Hercules are deeds performed for Eurystheus in exchange for restoring Hercules’ residence in Argos, and they bring fame lasting after death. They unfold through battles against the Nemean lion, Hydra, monsters, centaurs, giants, Amazons, Geryon, and the dragon, as well as captures and the relief of Atlas, purging sea and land of dangers. Though Lycus minimizes them, Amphitryon and the chorus praise Hercules’ courage; Hercules ultimately says his present disaster and his children’s deaths are more painful.

l: Hercules’ descent to the Underworld, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_for the hellhound Cerberus [to bring him into the daylight] Hercules descended through Taenarus to the realm of Pluto to bring the Underworld’s three-headed hound into the daylight. He has not yet returned, leaving his family exposed to Lycus.

l: the murder of Creon, Hecuba and other plays
s: Lycus murdered Creon and then seized the throne of Thebes. He threatens Creon’s daughter Megara and her children because he fears that they will avenge Creon’s death when they grow older.

l: the attempted execution of Megara, Amphitryon, and the children, Hecuba and other plays
s: The attempted execution of Megara, Amphitryon, and Hercules’ children is Lycus’ threatened collective killing of them. He plans to burn them at the altar, lets them enter Hercules’ house in funeral robes, and orders them to appear for death. As sacrifice seems imminent, Hercules returns, hides in the palace, confronts Lycus, and prevents the execution.

l: tyranny, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_exercised_by Lycus [over Thebes] Lycus embodies tyranny by seizing Thebes, silencing opposition, threatening the aged Chorus, and ordering the deaths of Megara and the children. The Chorus condemns him as an unworthy foreign ruler who governs through fear.

l: friendship and loyalty, Hecuba and other plays
s: Amphitryon, Megara, and the Chorus remain loyal to Hercules and his children despite danger. Amphitryon observes that misfortune exposes false friends, while the Chorus insists that friends are needed even when the dead can no longer defend their families.

l: honor and reputation, Hecuba and other plays
s: are_associated_with Hercules [his reputation is defended by Amphitryon] Amphitryon and the Chorus defend Hercules’ honor against Lycus’ accusation of cowardice. Amphitryon argues that skill with the bow can show prudence and courage, while Megara fears that dying in a shameful manner would dishonor their house.

l: Apollo, Hecuba and other plays
s: Apollo is a Pythian, oracular god worshipped at his temple at Delphi. He plays a lyre, laments Linus, and builds Troy’s paternal walls. He punishes and avenges Achilles’ son, whose killing at Apollo’s temple raises doubts about his justice.

l: Pelion, Hecuba and other plays
s: Peleus says he will go to the cave of Pelion after burying his grandson. It is associated with the place where he first received Thetis in his arms.

l: Mycenae, Hecuba and other plays
s: Mycenae is Eurystheus’s royal seat, ruled by him. From it he sends Copreus to reclaim Hercules’ children and leads his forces; its interests shape Hyllus’s proposed combat. It ends described through its famous walls, built by the Cyclops.

l: Hercules’ death, Hecuba and other plays
s: occurs_in the underworld [after he enters Pluto’s mansion] Hercules comes to Pluto’s mansion, called the house of tears and the goal of labour, where he is not expected to return. The Chorus describes his friends as dismayed and mourns his fate.

l: inveterate foes, Hecuba and other plays
s: threaten Hercules’ sons [with death] Megara says that she bore and nurtured her children only for them to become the scorn and sport of their inveterate foes, who are to cause their deaths.

l: Alcmena, Hecuba and other plays
s: Alcmena is a royal, aged Greek mother of Hercules and grandmother of his children. She defends the children when an Argive herald threatens to seize them, fears for their safety, and depends on foreign suppliants as Hyllus approaches with forces. After learning that her loved ones survived, the battle was won, and Iolaus regained youth, she confronts Eurystheus and seeks revenge for his persecution, ordering his death and the casting out of his corpse.

l: Hercules’ return from the Underworld, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hercules returns from the Underworld before Eurystheus knows that he has come back. He first goes to his household gods, bringing Cerberus from the Underworld and having rescued Theseus.

l: the death of Lycus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Lycus enters the palace intending to bring out Megara and the children, but Hercules ambushes and kills him. The Chorus hears his cries and celebrates his death as deserved.

l: Fiend, Hecuba and other plays
s: Fiend, daughter of Night, reluctantly serves Juno against Hercules, tries to dissuade Iris, then enters his house and unleashes madness and slaughter until Athena stops his violence.

l: murder of Hercules’ children and Megara, Hecuba and other plays
s: The murder of Hercules’ children and Megara is caused by Hercules’ madness during a purification ritual. In his frenzy, he kills Megara and his three children with arrows and a club until Athena stops him. The corpses leave him unable to perform burial rites and lead to his exile.

l: Hercules’ madness, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hercules’ madness, caused by Juno through the Fiend and linked to hydra venom, drives Hercules into delusions of fighting and traveling to Mycenae. In the frenzy he kills his children and Megara; awakening without memory, he later understands and mourns the killings.

l: Mount Aetna, Hecuba and other plays
s: Mount Ætna is a mountain in Sicily overlooking its plains, with rocky slopes and caves inhabited by Cyclops. It supplies Polyphemus’s feast implements; he hunts on its summit and is called its shepherd.

l: Cyclops, Hecuba and other plays
s: Cyclops are one-eyed sons of Neptune, shepherds living in caves without cities or shared government. They eat milk, cheese, sheep, and strangers, dwelling in Polyphemus’s cave, rejecting mutual rule and democracy.

l: Hercules’ exile, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hercules expects to be driven from his native Thebes and fears that no city or friend will accept him because of the killings. Theseus tells him to leave with him for Athens, and Hercules agrees to do so.

l: the burial of Hercules’ children, Hecuba and other plays
s: Amphitryon is instructed to consign the children’s bodies to the tomb and shed the required tears. Hercules says that their mother should embrace them in death, while he will later return to take Amphitryon to Athens.

l: purification from pollution, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_required_for Hercules [before entering Athens] Theseus promises that Hercules’ hands will be cleansed from pollution in Athens. This purification is presented as part of the refuge and assistance Athens will provide.

l: pollution, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hercules calls himself a source of contagion after killing his children and fears that no one will speak to him or allow him to enter a city. Theseus rejects the idea that a friend can transmit harm to another friend and offers to share Hercules’ condition.

l: friendship, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_valued_by Hercules [as steadfast support in misfortune] Theseus demonstrates friendship by coming to help Hercules despite his misfortune and by offering him refuge, wealth, purification, and lasting honor. Hercules concludes that a steadfast friend is more valuable than wealth or dominion.

l: suffering and misfortune, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hercules describes his suffering as greater than any previous labour and believes that no human being has endured more. Theseus answers that no person escapes the wounds of fortune and urges Hercules to bear what the gods have inflicted.

l: Iolaus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Iolaus is Hercules’ companion and comrade, an aged kinsman, friend, and warrior who becomes the surviving guardian of Hercules’ children after Hercules’ death. Though physically weakened and himself exiled from Argos, he travels with and protects the children, bringing them to Jupiter’s altar at Marathon and pleading with Demophoon and the Athenians against the Argive threat. He fears the oracle’s demand for a noble-born maiden, accepts Macaria’s voluntary sacrifice, and refuses to abandon the suppliants. When battle approaches, he arms himself, rides with Hyllus, prays to Hebe and Zeus, regains youthful strength through divine favor, pursues Eurystheus, and captures him alive near Scyron.

l: Copreus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Copreus is an Argive herald and emissary of Eurystheus who comes to seize Hercules’ children for Mycene, threatens Athens after Demophoon refuses, and withdraws promising armed return.

l: Demophoon, Hecuba and other plays
s: Demophoon is the constrained king and ruler of Athens, including Marathon, and a protector of suppliants. When Copreus seeks to remove the children of Hercules from the altar, he refuses, citing reverence, kinship, Hercules’ past services, and Athens’ honor. As Eurystheus and Argos approach, he summons citizens, arms Athens, and prepares sacrifices and lustrations. He will defend the foreign suppliants but refuses to sacrifice his daughter or any Athenian citizen, seeking a solution that saves Athens without public blame.

l: Macaria, Hecuba and other plays
s: Macaria, Hercules’ virgin daughter of noble birth, leaves her chamber after Iolaus’s lament and freely offers herself for death rather than be chosen by lot. Seeking heroic fame, she saves her brothers and Athens, requests proper rites and burial honors, and entrusts her family to survivors.

l: Chorus of Athenian old men, Hecuba and other plays
s: A group of elderly Athenian citizens protects Hercules’ suppliant children, condemns Copreus’ force, supports Demophoon’s refusal, and urges preparation for Argos’ threatened invasion.

l: Argives, Hecuba and other plays
s: Argives are an army of inhabitants and forces of Argos under Eurystheus, hostile to Athens over its protection of the children of Hercules. Represented by Copreus and Eurystheus, they demand the children’s return and threaten armed conflict. Numerous and fierce, they wait near Athens, attack, initially break through Athenian lines, then give way and are defeated and put to flight.

l: Athenians, Hecuba and other plays
s: protect children of Hercules [against Argive demands] The Athenians are portrayed as a free people who honor the gods and protect helpless suppliants. Demophoon expects them to resist Argos rather than surrender the children of Hercules, and he prepares their forces for the threatened conflict.

l: Marathon, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_a city in the Athenian dominions Marathon is the city in the Athenian dominions where the action takes place. The children of Hercules and Iolaus seek refuge there at the altar of Jupiter.

l: Argive invasion of Athens, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Argive invasion of Athens is a conflict between Athens and Argos, threatened after Copreus fails to seize the children of Hercules. Eurystheus promises an attack, prompting Demophoon to gather troops, spies, seers, and victims. As battle nears, Hyllus marshals Athens’ forces and Iolaus seeks to help despite age. After failed single combat and a virgin’s sacrifice, the armies fight; Athens ultimately routs Argos.

l: exile of the children of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays
s: The children of Hercules have been driven from their homeland and repeatedly expelled from places where they sought refuge because Eurystheus pursues them. Iolaus leads them to the Athenian realm, where they seek protection from further exile.

l: supplication at the altar, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_made_by children of Hercules [to obtain protection from their enemies] Iolaus and the children of Hercules sit before the altar of Jupiter with sacred branches and wreaths, asking not to be surrendered or forcibly removed. Their supplication is recognized by the Chorus and Demophoon as a claim that the gods and the laws of Athens must protect.

l: execution decree against the children, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_issued_by Argos [against the children of Hercules] Copreus claims that the laws of Argos ordered the children of Hercules to bleed and that he has come to enforce that sentence. Iolaus counters that the children were banished from their native land and therefore cannot justly be reclaimed as its subjects.

l: protection of the suppliants, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_provided_by Demophoon [in defense of the altar and Athens] Demophoon undertakes to protect the children of Hercules from Eurystheus and refuses to let Copreus remove them. He treats their protection as required by the gods, kinship, gratitude for Hercules’ services, and the honor of Athens.

l: freedom of Athens, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_defended_by Demophoon [against Argos] The freedom of Athens is connected with its refusal to surrender suppliants through fear of Argos. Demophoon declares that Athens will maintain its independence rather than become an appendage of the Argive realm.

l: Hyllus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hyllus, son of Hercules, leads the Athenian army, challenges Eurystheus for the sons of Hercules and hereditary rank, then fights successfully and raises trophies with Iolaus.

l: the oracles, Hecuba and other plays
s: require Macaria’s sacrifice [to save Athens and the suppliants] The oracles give differing instructions on the city’s situation, but all the relevant auspices agree that Ceres requires the sacrifice of a blooming maiden born to a noble father. Their response creates the crisis that Demophoon and the suppliants must resolve.

l: Athenian army, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Athenian army assembles to resist the Argive forces, with chiefs informed and its left wing formed after victims are removed. Ready for battle, it fights for its land and reputation, defeats the Argive army, and contributes to Eurystheus’s capture.

l: the foreign suppliants, Hecuba and other plays
s: The foreign suppliants are the children of Hercules, Iolaus, and Alcmena, who seek protection in Athens from Argos. Their presence places Athens in danger, but Demophoon and the Chorus argue that the city must not betray guests who have appealed for aid.

l: Macaria’s sacrifice, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_a voluntary offering [made by Macaria] Macaria’s sacrifice is required by the oracles as the means of saving the city and the suppliants. She freely accepts this role, refuses to be chosen by lot, requests female attendants and proper rites, and departs to die for her brothers and Athens.

l: the threat to Athens, Hecuba and other plays
s: The threat to Athens comes from the approaching forces of Argos and Eurystheus. The city faces both foreign attack and possible civil conflict over whether to protect the suppliants, while the required sacrifice is presented as the means of averting destruction.

l: glory and reputation in war, Hecuba and other plays
s: A topic concerning honor and fame in war: Macaria gains lasting glory through willing death for her brothers, while generals’ credit is challenged against soldiers’ suffering, and the Chorus warns that victory won unjustly yields fading, shameful renown.

l: death, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_a cure [for mortal suffering according to the wise] Death is presented by Macaria as preferable to dishonor, abandonment, and captivity. She embraces a firm and voluntary death for a glorious cause, while Iolaus says that the wise have regarded death as the most effective cure for every ill.

l: Servant, Hecuba and other plays
s: A messenger reports the Athenian army’s victory, recounts the battle and Eurystheus’s capture, then asks Alcmene to honor her promise and free him.

l: Messenger, Hecuba and other plays
s: leads Eurystheus [as a captive to Alcmene] The Messenger brings Eurystheus before Alcmene and reports that Hyllus and Iolaus have captured him. He warns that the rulers of Athens forbid the killing of a captive taken alive in battle.

l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays
s: A choral group celebrates victory, reversal, Zeus's justice, and Hercules among the gods; it urges Alcmene to release Eurystheus, then approves his killing.

l: single combat, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_proposed_by Hyllus [against Eurystheus] Hyllus proposes single combat with Eurystheus to settle the conflict and determine the fate of the sons of Hercules. Eurystheus refuses to face him, so the armies proceed to battle.

l: Iolaus's rejuvenation, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_granted_by Hebe [for one day through divine intervention] Iolaus's rejuvenation occurs after he prays to Hebe and Zeus while pursuing Eurystheus. Hercules and Hebe are seen as stars above his chariot, and Iolaus temporarily regains the strength of youth.

l: capture of Eurystheus, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_accomplished_by Iolaus [after the Athenian victory] After the battle, the rejuvenated Iolaus pursues Eurystheus, seizes him in his chariot near the rocks of Scyron, binds him with chains, and brings him before Alcmene.

l: death of Eurystheus, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_intended_by Alcmene [as revenge] Alcmene orders Eurystheus to be killed in revenge for his crimes, despite Athens's rule against killing a captive taken alive. Eurystheus accepts that she may destroy him and says that his death will give Athens the protection foretold by the oracle.

l: oracle of Phoebus, Hecuba and other plays
s: foretells Eurystheus [as a guardian of Athens after burial] The oracle of Phoebus declares that Eurystheus's corpse must be buried near the temple of the Pallenian maid. It promises that he will protect Athens after death and harm the descendants of the race he detests when they attack the city.

l: laws of Greece, Hecuba and other plays
s: forbid death of Eurystheus [after his capture alive in battle] Eurystheus argues that the laws of Greece protect a captive who was not killed during battle. The Messenger and Eurystheus both state that killing him after his capture would stain the person responsible with lasting guilt.

l: Rhesus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Rhesus is a Thracian king, son of Strymon and the Muse, who rules Thrace and Pæonia, receives tribute from Scythians, and commands a Thracian host. A kinsman of Hector and raised to the throne by him, he comes late in the war’s tenth year to aid Troy after conflict with the Scythians. He arrives in a car drawn by famed white horses, with golden armor and shield, promising to destroy the Greeks and return home the next day.
