Ulysses and Diomede kill him in a night attack while he sleeps. The Muse later declares that he will be restored as a god and priest of Bacchus.

l: Aeneas, Hecuba and other plays
s: A Trojan warrior advises Hector that Greek campfires may be a stratagem, warns against a night attack, and urges sending a voluntary spy while offering support if needed.

l: Dolon, Hecuba and other plays
s: Dolon is a Trojan spy serving Hector and Troy. He volunteers for a nocturnal reconnaissance of the Greek fleet, wearing a wolf disguise for covert movement and seeking Achilles’ steeds as reward. He boasts of returning before sunrise, perhaps with Ulysses’ or Diomede’s head, but later remains absent, prompting fear that he has fallen into an ambush.

l: Diomede, Hecuba and other plays
s: Greek warrior, son of Tydeus, joins Ulysses in the Trojan camp, kills Thracian soldiers, and escapes after Rhesus is slain.

l: the Muse, Hecuba and other plays
s: One of nine sisters and Rhesus’s grieving mother, the Muse mourns his death, recounts his origins, blames Minerva, and prophesies his restoration to divine life.

l: the charioteer of Rhesus, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_wounded_in Rhesus’s death [while defending his master] Rhesus’s charioteer wakes to the sound of dying men, sees Rhesus bleeding, and is wounded while trying to find weapons. He survives, accuses Hector of murdering the Thracians for their horses, and is taken to Hector’s house for treatment.

l: Chorus of Trojan sentinels, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Chorus of Trojan sentinels guards the Trojan camp at night and reports activity in the Greek camp. It wakes Hector over fires and tumult, urges caution, supports sending a spy and Dolon, and celebrates Rhesus. It fails to detect Ulysses and Diomede, later challenges them, and accepts Ulysses after the watchword Apollo.

l: the Trojan army, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Trojan army is ordered to prepare its weapons when the Greek camp appears to be in motion. Hector later tells the troops to remain ready to follow the summons of the trumpet if the Greeks begin to flee.

l: the Trojan camp, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_threatened_by Rhesus’s Thracian army [if Rhesus survives the night] The Trojan camp is entered by Ulysses and Diomede during the night. Rhesus’s troops are placed there, but the camp’s guards fail to prevent the raid and are later ordered to prepare for battle.

l: the Greek flight, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Greek flight is suspected because fires blaze throughout the Greek camp and near the fleet. Hector is prepared to attack if the Greeks are departing, but the Chorus and Aeneas note that their actual intention has not yet been established.

l: the nocturnal spying mission, Hecuba and other plays
s: The nocturnal spying mission is proposed by Aeneas and undertaken by Dolon. Its purpose is to discover whether the Greeks intend to flee or to ensnare the Trojans.

l: Menelaus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Menelaus is a Greek king, Spartan leader, son of Atreus, brother of Agamemnon, lawful husband of Helen, and father of Hermione. He leads Greeks against Troy, saying that his purpose is to punish Paris for violating hospitality and taking Helen rather than merely to fight for a woman. After Troy’s destruction, he intends to take Helen to Greece and have her killed, though he agrees not to bring her onto his own ship. Accounts initially report that he and Helen are dead after the Greek fleet is scattered by a storm. In fact, he is shipwrecked, impoverished, and separated from his ships after years of wandering. In Egypt he learns that the Helen brought from Troy was a phantom, reunites with the real Helen, disguises himself as a shipwrecked mariner, and spreads the false report of his own death. Armed and supported by surviving sailors, he deceives Theoclymenus, seizes a ship, defeats Egyptian sailors, and sails toward Greece with Helen. Later, as Hermione’s father and a ruler with power over others, he assists Hermione against Andromache. He threatens Molossus to force Andromache from Thetis’s altar, seeks the deaths of both mother and son, and claims authority based on having taken Andromache at Troy and on her connection to Hermione. Peleus subdues him, however, and Menelaus flees toward Sparta, leaving Hermione behind while intending to lead forces and later confront Neoptolemus.

l: Hermes, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hermes carries Helen through the air, conceals her, and leaves her with Proteus in Egypt so she remains undefiled and returns to Sparta with Menelaus.

l: Achilles’ steeds, Hecuba and other plays
s: Achilles’ immortal, divinely descended horses, given by Neptune to Peleus, are promised by Hector to Dolon as payment for spying.

l: Dolon’s wolf disguise, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_a wolf disguise [made from a slain wolf’s hide and visage] Dolon’s wolf disguise consists of a tawny wolf hide, a hairy animal face covering, and arrangements for his hands and legs to imitate the beast’s movement. He intends to use it to approach the Greek trenches and ramparts without being discovered.

l: Ajax, Hecuba and other plays
s: Ajax, a Greek chief and Teucer’s brother, dies on his own sword after another warrior receives Achilles’ arms, causing Teucer’s exile.

l: Phrygians, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Phrygians, the people of Troy, fight alongside allies during the siege, while Hector trusts Rhesus to strike the Greek fleet. They disapprove of Deiphobus taking Helen by force, but the Greeks destroy and occupy their city and temples, slaughter and enslave their women, defeat them, and order them to the Greek navy to sail from their land.

l: Trojan walls, Hecuba and other plays
s: are_under_siege_by Greek fleet [during the siege of Troy] The Trojan walls are the defenses of the city that Rhesus promises to overthrow. Hector says that Rhesus may choose a position on the left wing, right wing, or centre near the front of the fighting.

l: Rhesus’s arrival at Troy, Hecuba and other plays
s: Rhesus’s arrival at Troy follows a delayed journey caused by war with the Scythians near the Euxine. He says that he crossed the Hellespont and marched through various lands without resting in luxury before reaching Troy.

l: Dolon’s reconnaissance, Hecuba and other plays
s: targets Greek fleet Dolon’s reconnaissance concerns the Greek fleet and has kept him away from the Trojan lines. Hector and the Chorus await his report, but the unit ends before he returns.

l: night watch, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_organized_by Trojans [in successive divisions] The night watch changes according to assigned divisions, with different groups guarding the ramparts and Lycia’s warriors due to be roused. The Chorus notes that the night is ending as the Pleiades rise and dawn approaches.

l: warfare and conquest, Hecuba and other plays
s: Rhesus describes warfare and conquest as the means by which he will rescue Troy, seize Greek spoils, and later ravage Greece. Hector considers the conquest of Argos and the Greek states far less easy than Rhesus claims.

l: Thetis, Hecuba and other plays
s: Thetis is a goddess, daughter of Nereus and sister of the Nereids, who lived with and was wife of Peleus and mother of Achilles. Her marriage is revered in a temple and altar. After withdrawing from human dwellings, she counsels Peleus, orders Achilles’ son buried at Delphi, sends Andromache and her son to Molossia, and makes Peleus immortal.

l: Rhesus’s Thracian army, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_destroyed_in Rhesus’s death [during the night attack] Rhesus’s Thracian army is stationed outside the Trojan lines and sleeps without adequate sentinels or properly arranged arms. Ulysses and Diomede destroy the force’s leadership and leave the army utterly ruined.

l: Rhesus’s car, Hecuba and other plays
s: Rhesus’s car stands beside his sleeping place with the Thracian horses yoked to it. Ulysses and Diomede seize the car after killing Rhesus.

l: Rhesus’s white horses, Hecuba and other plays
s: Rhesus’s white horses are described as having coats like swan feathers and as unmatched in beauty. Minerva directs Ulysses and Diomede to carry them away as a glorious prize, and the charioteer says that the raiders escaped with them.

l: Rhesus’s death, Hecuba and other plays
s: occurs_in the Trojan night raid Rhesus’s death occurs when Ulysses and Diomede attack his sleeping camp during the night. The Muse mourns it, Hector orders that his body be buried with honor, and the Muse declares that he will later be restored to divine life.

l: the Trojan night raid, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_conducted_by Ulysses [with Diomede] The Trojan night raid is carried out by Ulysses and Diomede against Rhesus and the Thracians. It kills Rhesus, devastates his army, and ends with the raiders escaping through the alerted Trojan camp.

l: Rhesus’s funeral and apotheosis, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_promised_for Rhesus [with funeral honors and divine elevation] Hector orders that Rhesus and the other dead be interred with due respect, while he plans to honor Rhesus with a tomb and rich garments. The Muse says that Rhesus will not remain in an ordinary grave but will be restored to life as a god, priest of Bacchus and of the deity worshipped beneath Pangaeum.

l: Andromache, Hecuba and other plays
s: Andromache is a woman from Thebes, formerly queen of Troy, wife and later widow of Hector, and mother of Astyanax. After Troy is destroyed, she sees Hector slain and Astyanax thrown from the city’s towers. Taken among the Trojan spoils, she is carried to Greece as a captive and slave, grieving the loss of Troy and unable to bury Astyanax herself before leaving with Neoptolemus, who chooses her and forces her into his household and marriage. In Phthia she bears Neoptolemus a son, Molossus, while remaining marked by captivity and the death of her first husband and child. When Hermione accuses her of using magic drugs and, aided by Menelaus, seeks to kill her and Molossus, Andromache takes sanctuary at Thetis’ temple. She denies the accusation, stresses that she was forced into her master’s bed, and submits to death to save Molossus. Torn from the altar and led toward execution with her son, she appeals to Peleus, who frees and protects them, though she fears renewed violence. At the end, Thetis directs her to marry Helenus and live in Molossia; through her, a surviving royal line connected with Aeacus will continue.

l: the Trojan Horse, Hecuba and other plays
s: A wooden vehicle built by Epeus under Minerva’s inspiration conceals armed Greeks; mistaken for a sacred peace pledge, it enters Troy and admits the force that destroys the city.

l: lottery assigning the captives, Hecuba and other plays
s: The lottery assigning the captives determines separate Greek masters for the Trojan women. Cassandra goes to Agamemnon, Andromache to Achilles’ son, Hecuba to Ulysses, and Polyxena to Achilles’ tomb.

l: storm and dispersal of the Greek fleet, Hecuba and other plays
s: After Troy fell, Neptune causes a storm with violent waves and whirlpools that disperses the Greek fleet in the Aegean Sea; Menelaus’s fate is unknown.

l: Cassandra’s prophecy, Hecuba and other plays
s: Cassandra’s prophecy foretells Agamemnon’s destruction, the fall of the Atreus house, her own death, and Ulysses’ prolonged and perilous journey home. She also predicts that the Greeks will suffer more deeply than the Trojans despite their victory.

l: Astyanax, Hecuba and other plays
s: Astyanax is the child and son of Hector and Andromache, grandson of Hecuba, and the only one of Andromache’s loved ones remaining in Troy. After Troy is captured, the Greeks sentence him to death because he is Hector’s son, fearing he might grow up and rebuild Troy. Andromache gives him a final embrace and kiss before he is taken away. He is thrown from Troy’s towers or walls, killed, and his disfigured body is brought to Hecuba. He is buried in Hector’s shield, with a tomb prepared after his death.

l: Salamis, Hecuba and other plays
s: Salamis is Teucer’s native land, from which he was banished by Telamon. Teucer says that he is destined to settle in Cyprus and name the walls he builds Salamis in memory of his homeland.

l: Astyanax’s execution, Hecuba and other plays
s: Astyanax’s execution, ordered by the Greeks after Ulysses argues Hector’s son must not be raised, follows Troy’s fall: Andromache bids farewell before he is thrown from Troy’s towers.

l: Hector’s death, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hector’s death in the Trojan War, caused by Achilles, leaves Andromache widowed and contributes to her enslavement; his body is dragged around Troy, and his fame endangers Astyanax.

l: the bridal marriage of Paris and Helen, Hecuba and other plays
s: The marriage associated with Paris and Helen is blamed for Troy’s suffering. Hecuba says that through one woman’s nuptials she has borne dreadful ills, and the Chorus calls Paris’ espousals accursed.

l: the Trojan royal house, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_destroyed the fall of Troy [along with the city] The Trojan royal house is destroyed through the deaths of Priam, Hector, the royal sons, and the royal daughters. Hecuba, once queen, is reduced to an aged slave, while Astyanax is killed before he can inherit or rebuild Troy.

l: the wooden horse deception, Hecuba and other plays
s: deceives the Trojans [by presenting the horse as a holy image and pledge of peace] The wooden horse deception causes the fall of Troy. The Greeks conceal armed men inside the wooden structure, while the Trojans bring it into the city as a sacred offering and celebrate without recognizing the trap.

l: hope, Hecuba and other plays
s: persists life [while life remains] Andromache says that hope visits other sufferers but never comes to her, because no promised joy remains. Hecuba says that fair hope cannot be entirely extinguished while life remains, though her own circumstances leave little room for it.

l: grief and mourning, Hecuba and other plays
s: Grief and mourning are a relief for sufferers, expressed through tears and lamentation over the dead, burning city, lost family, and separated mothers and children; they dominate Hecuba, Andromache, and the Chorus, then extend to Helen, Greek wives, and war’s suffering.

l: death, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_a release_from_sorrow [for the dead] Death takes Priam, Hector, the Trojan sons, Polyxena, and many Trojan youths. Andromache says death is preferable to a life of misery, while Hecuba reflects that the dead no longer suffer or weep.

l: Castor, Hecuba and other plays
s: Castor, Zeus's divinized twin son by Leda and Helen's brother, appears with Pollux, stops Theoclymenus's attack, affirms Helen's return to Menelaus, and promises sea guidance.

l: Pollux, Hecuba and other plays
s: Pollux, Zeus’s divine twin son of Leda and Helen’s brother, appears with Castor, calms Theoclymenus, and foretells Helen’s return and divine honors.

l: the Grecian host, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Grecian host fights Troy, believing Paris took Helen and seeking to punish violated hospitality. It destroys Paris and Troy, though many die for Helen’s phantom. After victory, it entrusts Helen’s fate to Menelaus, while surviving companions await orders near Egypt.

l: women, Hecuba and other plays
s: Women are presented as subject to a proposed law that any woman who betrays her husband should die. Menelaus says that Helen’s ruin should warn all women to be chaste.

l: Helen’s defense, Hecuba and other plays
s: Helen’s defense claims that divine influence, Paris, Priam, and force rather than her own will caused her departure from Sparta and her life in Troy. She also says that she tried to escape after Paris’s death but was prevented by the guards and later forced into marriage by Deiphobus.

l: Hecuba’s accusation of Helen, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hecuba’s accusation states that Helen willingly chose Paris because of his beauty and Troy’s wealth, remained in Paris’s household by choice, and followed Fortune rather than virtue. Hecuba says that Helen refused repeated advice to flee and shows no remorse for the war.

l: Helen’s execution, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_planned_by Menelaus [after transport to Argos] Menelaus first says that Helen will be stoned or killed in Greece to atone for the woes of Greece. He orders her taken to the ships and later states that she will be slain in Argos, although she will not travel in his own vessel.

l: the Greek navy, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Greek navy is the place to which the Phrygians must proceed before sailing from the ruined land. One ship remains to carry the spoils and captives onward.

l: Hector’s shield, Hecuba and other plays
s: Hector’s brazen, refulgent shield guarded his arm in battle, bears his shape, and is given to Hecuba, who wreathes it for Astyanax’s burial.

l: the body of Astyanax, Hecuba and other plays
s: The body of Astyanax is brought in on Hector’s shield after Talthybius has washed it and cleansed its wounds. Hecuba adorns the disfigured corpse with garments, wreaths, and fillets before it is taken to the grave.

l: the burning of Troy, Hecuba and other plays
s: The burning of Troy is the city’s complete, irrevocable ruin in a war over a woman. It begins when Talthybius orders troops to cast torches into Troy; flames consume its roofs, streets, palace, and towers, killing Phrygian rulers and warriors and leaving blazing ruins, enslavement, and loss.

l: the murder of Astyanax, Hecuba and other plays
s: The murder of Astyanax is condemned as an unexampled and cowardly act committed by Greeks who feared a child’s possible future power. Hecuba imagines the shameful epitaph that the Greeks, fearing the infant, killed him.

l: funeral rites for Astyanax, Hecuba and other plays
s: Astyanax’s funeral rites wash, cleanse, adorn, and bury the child in Hector’s shield, while Talthybius and Greek troops prepare the grave and Hecuba and Chorus lament.

l: Hecuba’s grief, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_caused_by the murder of Astyanax [and the destruction of Troy] Hecuba’s grief appears in her lament for Astyanax, her memories of his childhood, and her condemnation of the Greeks who killed him. Her grief expands to include Hector, Priam, her lost children, the burning of Troy, and her enslavement far from home.

l: Silenus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Silenus is a satyr, devoted follower of Bacchus and father of the Chorus of Satyrs. Captured with his sons while seeking Bacchus, he becomes Polypheme’s enslaved shepherd, servant, and cupbearer. He trades wine to Ulysses for food, aids the Greeks, deceives Polypheme, serves him wine while drinking himself, claims to be Ganymede, and flees before the attack.

l: Chorus of Satyrs, Hecuba and other plays
s: A chorus of satyr children enslaved as Polypheme's herdsmen, it mourns separation from Bacchus, conceals Greeks, discusses Trojan War with Ulysses, and fears Polypheme will eat them.

l: Polypheme the Cyclops, Hecuba and other plays
s: Polypheme is a one-eyed, savage Cyclops, son of Neptune, who rules and lives in the Cyclops’ caves on Mount Ætna with his flocks. He eats animals, strangers, and Ulysses’ companions, rejects hospitality and the gods’ authority, and values wealth and bodily pleasure. Armed with a club, he orders Ulysses and the strangers prepared as food, then feasts, drinks wine, and falls asleep. Ulysses and his companions blind him with a burning brand. Polypheme recognizes Ulysses, recalls the oracle, and threatens him and his crew.

l: Sicily, Hecuba and other plays
s: contains Mount Ætna Sicily contains Mount Ætna, where the Cyclops live in isolated caves. Ulysses and his crew are driven to its coast by storms after leaving Troy.

l: ship (Ulysses’ ship), Hecuba and other plays
s: Ulysses’ ship, driven by storms from near Troy, is stranded on Sicily; his men leave it for Polypheme’s cave and hope to escape in it.

l: Polyphemus’s cave, Hecuba and other plays
s: Polyphemus’s cave is a rocky cave on Mount Ætna and the Cyclops’s dwelling, where Silenus and the Satyrs serve. It holds provisions, furnishings, cooking implements, wine, and an olive pole. Ulysses and his men enter for food, face threats and feasting on companions, then prepare escape and an attack.

l: wine (Bacchus’s wine), Hecuba and other plays
s: Bacchus’s wine is Maron’s unmingled gift, carried by Ulysses and associated with Bacchus. Silenus trades cheese and lambs for it and drinks eagerly. Ulysses repeatedly gives it to Polyphemus, who becomes drunk, staggers, sees visions, and sleeps, enabling his blinding.

l: cannibalism, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_practiced_by Polypheme the Cyclops [through the eating of human flesh] Polypheme practices cannibalism, saying that he has not tasted human flesh for a long time and intends to eat Ulysses and his companions. The Chorus condemns his practice of roasting and devouring suppliants in his cave.

l: Cyclopes, Hecuba and other plays
s: are_brothers_of Polyphemus [fellow Cyclopes] Polyphemus intends to go and revel with his Cyclopean brothers, but Ulysses persuades him to remain alone with the wine. The Chorus speaks of escaping the Cyclopes’ region and returning to Grecian maids.

l: Grecian companions, Hecuba and other plays
s: are_eaten_at the Cyclops’s feast [by Polyphemus] Two of Ulysses’ fattest Grecian companions are seized and killed by Polyphemus, who roasts part of one and boils the other. The surviving companions hide in the cave’s recesses and later help Ulysses carry out his plan.

l: Sicilia, Hecuba and other plays
s: contains the Cyclops’ cave [as the region where it is located] Ulysses says that he will steer his vessel to his country across Sicilia’s waves.

l: olive pole, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_used_for the blinding of Polyphemus [heated and driven into the eye] An olive pole lying in the cave is heated in the fire until it flames. Ulysses and his companions use it as a burning lever to pierce and destroy Polyphemus’s eyesight.

l: the Cyclops’s eye, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_burned_out_by the blinding of Polyphemus [with a heated brand] The Cyclops’s eye is pierced and burned by the heated brand. Polyphemus is deprived of his eyesight and can no longer see Ulysses and his companions, though he remains able to threaten them.

l: the vessel, Hecuba and other plays
s: A wine-filled drinking vessel, kept privately by Polyphemus, is brought from the cave by Ulysses and served to Polyphemus after he agrees not to share it.

l: the Cyclops’s feast, Hecuba and other plays
s: includes Grecian companions [as victims consumed by Polyphemus] The Cyclops’s feast consists of the flesh of Ulysses’ companions, along with milk and wine. Polyphemus’s feast leaves him glutted and intoxicated, making possible Ulysses’ attack.

l: the blinding of Polyphemus, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_caused_by Ulysses [as requital for the murder of his companions] The blinding of Polyphemus is accomplished through Ulysses’ craft, wine, sleep, and a heated olive pole. The Chorus celebrates the deed but avoids directly undertaking the dangerous work.

l: the voyage home, Hecuba and other plays
s: The voyage home is Ulysses’s planned sea journey from Polyphemus toward his country, carrying his companions, the Chorus, its friends, and its sire despite threatened rocks and violence.

l: Teucer, Hecuba and other plays
s: Teucer, son of Telamon and a Greek warrior from Salamis, fights in the Trojan War. After Troy’s fall and Ajax’s death, he reaches Egypt seeking Theonoe’s prophecy about a voyage to Cyprus, encounters Helen, and is destined to settle in Salamis there.

l: Chorus of Grecian dames, Hecuba and other plays
s: The Chorus of Grecian dames, Helen’s Grecian attendants and companions, mourns her sufferings and Troy’s destruction, counsels her to seek Theonoe’s truth, and accompanies her palaceward. Astonished by Menelaus’s deception, it restrains Theoclymenus, defends pious Theonoe, and accepts the divine explanation.

l: the Messenger, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_a messenger [reporting the escape and battle] The Messenger reports that Helen has departed from Egypt with Menelaus. He describes Menelaus’s deception, the preparations for the voyage, the battle aboard the ship, and his own escape by lowering himself into the sea and being rescued by a rope.

l: Theoclymenus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Theoclymenus is Proteus’s son, Theonoe’s brother, and king of Egypt, ruling after his father’s death from a palace before which Proteus’s tomb stands. Dutifully devoted to the gods, he nevertheless seeks Helen as his bride despite her fidelity to Menelaus and kills captured Greek strangers. While away hunting, he has ordered Theonoe to report Menelaus’s arrival and would kill Menelaus if discovered. Believing Menelaus dead, he aids Helen’s supposed funeral rites, supplying a Tyrian fifty-oared bark, sailors, and gifts while still planning their marriage. After Helen escapes with Menelaus, he blames and tries to kill Theonoe, but the Chorus and the Dioscuri intervene; he spares her and permits Helen’s return home.

l: Theonoe, Hecuba and other plays
s: Theonoe is a prophetic woman, daughter of Proteus and of Nereus’s line, whose divine knowledge reveals past, present, and future. She knows Menelaus has survived, reached Egypt, and is destined, with Helen, for a safe return to Sparta despite Venus’s opposition. When Helen and Menelaus seek her counsel, she places justice, the gods, and her father’s honor above loyalty to her brother Theoclymenus. She conceals Menelaus’s arrival, withholds the truth from Theoclymenus, protects Helen and Menelaus, and urges their escape. Theoclymenus later accuses her of silence, but the Dioscuri affirm that her piety and obedience to the gods made her choice wise.

l: Nile, Hecuba and other plays
s: waters Egypt The Nile’s bright virgin currents water Egypt’s soil and are supplied by molten snow rather than rain. Its banks are the setting in which Helen speaks and Teucer arrives.

l: Egypt, Hecuba and other plays
s: Egypt is the Nile-watered land where Proteus ruled, his son's palace stands, and Hermes placed Helen while Menelaus and the Greek forces fought at Troy. Later Theoclymenus rules there, holding Helen and the shipwrecked Menelaus. They plan and escape with his companions in a Sidonian bark, as Egyptian sailors lose control during the voyage.

l: Pharos, Hecuba and other plays
s: is_a island [at the mouth of the Nile] Pharos is the island at the mouth of the Nile where Proteus lived and ruled. The scene is set at Proteus’ tomb near the entrance to Theoclymenus’ palace there.

l: Proteus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Proteus was a virtuous king who ruled Egypt and lived on Pharos. Hermes placed Helen in his house to keep her undefiled. After he died, he was buried in a tomb before the palace gate; his son Theoclymenus and daughter Theonoe remained. Theoclymenus addresses his tomb and seeks to marry Helen, while Proteus’ hostility toward Greeks persists after their arrival.

l: Leda, Hecuba and other plays
s: Leda, Helen’s mother, reportedly bore Helen from an egg after Zeus approached her as a swan, then died by hanging, possibly connected to Helen’s supposed guilt.

l: Helen’s phantom, Hecuba and other plays
s: Helen’s phantom is a living image or cloud resembling Helen, made from ether and secretly formed in her likeness. It was created by divine power, attributed to Hera, Juno, and the son of Maia, to keep Paris from obtaining or marrying the real Helen, who remained in Egypt. Given to Paris and taken to Troy in Helen’s place, it was believed to be Helen and became the object connected with the Trojan War. Menelaus later took it from Troy, believing it his wife; it was associated with his ships and guarded in a cave by his surviving companions. It then declared that it had been substituted for the real Helen, vanished, and returned to the ether or sky. The Dioscuri also say it was secretly conveyed to an island near the Athenian realm.

l: Helen’s beauty, Hecuba and other plays
s: causes Trojan War [through the Judgment of Paris] Helen’s beauty caused Aphrodite to win the judgment of Paris by promising her to him. Helen regards her beauty as a source of ruin rather than blessing because it brought war and caused her false reputation.

l: Helen’s false reputation, Hecuba and other plays
s: Helen is widely believed to have betrayed Menelaus and caused the Trojan War, although she says that she never went to Troy and committed no wrongdoing. Teucer initially condemns her because of this reputation before learning that she is not the Helen he saw at Troy.

l: tomb of Proteus, Hecuba and other plays
s: Proteus’ tomb is a burial place at the entrance of Theoclymenus’ palace in Pharos, with a surrounding trench and burning altars. Helen kneels there to seek protection for her marriage, mourn Menelaus, and find refuge. After learning Menelaus lives, she meets him there; the tomb shelters him from the king’s force, hosts Helen’s supplication to Theonoe, and becomes the starting place of their deception and threatened joint death.
